title: Revisiting the 16× Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models

paper.title: Revisiting the 16 × 16\times Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion language models (DLMs) have attracted wide attention for their fast, parallel decoding, but they are believed to be far less efficient to train than autoregressive language models (ARMs): a widely cited study reports that a DLM needs roughly 16 × 16\times the training compute of an ARM to match its likelihood, a figure that has made pretraining DLMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model’s own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder–decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 1{,}700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8 × 12.8\times ; block diffusion training and an encoder–decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8 × 7.8\times at block size 32 32 , and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6 × 4.6\times at block size 8 8 and 3.0 × 3.0\times at block size 4 4 . We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder–decoder block diffusion, a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. Overall, the 16 × 16\times figure substantially overstates the pretraining cost gap between DLMs and ARMs, and pretraining DLMs from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have become the leading non-autoregressive alternative for language modeling ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2023 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Ou et al., 2025 ; Nie et al., 2026 ) . Their appeal is fast, parallel generation: open-weight masked diffusion language models report about 2.5 × 2.5\times the generation throughput of autoregressive language models (ARMs) at comparable accuracy ( Wu et al., 2026a ; Reda et al., 2026 ) , with commercial systems reporting up to 10 × 10\times ( Labs et al., 2025 ) . Yet, their training efficiency is widely believed to be far worse than that of ARMs. The most cited quantification is the IsoFLOP study of Nie et al. (2025) (SMDM), which concludes that an MDM needs about 16 × 16\times the training FLOPs of an ARM to reach the same validation perplexity, and the number is now routinely quoted as a property of the MDM family. This 16 × 16\times figure has made pretraining MDMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. Taking a closer look at how this 16 × 16\times figure was achieved, however, we find that the methodology behind it has fallen out of step with current practice of diffusion language modeling. SMDM measured it on a full-sequence, decoder-only MDM scored with its negative evidence lower bound (ELBO), all three of which now have alternatives. First, the ELBO is an upper bound on the negative log-likelihood (NLL), and it scores the model under uniformly random token orders it never uses at inference; in contrast, DUEL ( Turok et al., 2026 ) computes the exact NLL of a diffusion model under the custom decoding order it is deployed with. Second, nearly all of today’s large-scale diffusion language models (DLMs) use block-wise factorization ( Arriola et al., 2025 , BD3LM;) with block sizes between 4 4 and 32 32 , rather than operating over the full sequence. Third, encoder–decoder architectures that separate the processing of clean and noised tokens ( Arriola et al., 2026 , E2D2;) offer computationally cheaper training than the decoder-only network. While the papers that introduce these techniques compare a handful of models at fixed sizes, none of these has been measured under a rigorous compute-matched IsoFLOP analysis. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of masked diffusion models with a protocol that implements the ideas above: we score every diffusion model using the exact likelihood induced by its top-1 confidence decoding rule, utilize block-aware training and an encoder–decoder architecture, and sweep the block sizes b ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{4,8,16,32\} which are commonly used in practice. In addition, we make two corrections to the SMDM protocol: we count training FLOPs exactly, including the output head and attention computation, and we read compute multiples within the measured range of the scaling laws rather than by extrapolation. Under this new protocol we study ten model variants and train about 1,700 1{,}700 models in total; to our knowledge, this is the largest compute-matched scaling analysis of diffusion language models to date. With this analysis, we find that pretraining diffusion language models is far cheaper than previously thought (Figure 1 ). Scored with the ELBO, our full-sequence MDM lands close to the published figure, at 17.8 × 17.8\times . Scoring the very same checkpoints with the exact likelihood lowers the multiple to 12.8 × 12.8\times . Block diffusion training and the encoder–decoder architecture then reduce it further to 7.8 × 7.8\times at block size 32 32 , and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6 × 4.6\times at block size 8 8 and 3.0 × 3.0\times at block size 4 4 . In addition, we find that the optimal decoder depth of encoder–decoder block diffusion follows a simple rule that depends on the block size alone, that the gap between E2D2 and the ARM holds at a held-out budget three times larger than our largest fitted FLOPs, and that likelihood improvements carry over to downstream accuracy. Our contributions are the following. (i) We revisit the scaling laws of diffusion language models under a revised protocol that reflects recent advances: exact likelihood evaluation, block diffusion, encoder–decoder models, and a sweep over practically used block sizes. (ii) We show that, under this protocol, pretraining diffusion language models is far cheaper than the 16 × 16\times suggests: exact likelihood evaluation reduces the compute multiple to 12.8 × 12.8\times , block diffusion training with an encoder–decoder architecture reduces it to 7.8 × 7.8\times at b = 32 b{=}32 , and smaller block sizes further narrow it to 4.6 × 4.6\times at b = 8 b{=}8 and 3.0 × 3.0\times at b = 4 b{=}4 . (iii) We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder–decoder block diffusion, which depends on the block size alone; a held-out budget at 3 × 10 20 3{\times}10^{20} FLOPs, at which the gap between E2D2 and the ARM persists; and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to downstream accuracy.

Prior scaling studies ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Von Rütte et al., 2026 ; Ni et al., 2025b ) evaluate a trained MDM by a Monte-Carlo estimate of Eq. 1 and compare it with the exact NLL of an ARM. This comparison is problematic in two respects. First, Eq. 1 is only an upper bound on the NLL; how far it lies from the NLL, and how this varies across models, is poorly understood. sections.text: Turok et al. (2026) address both points. Let π \pi be a deterministic unmasking rule that, given the tokens unmasked so far, selects the next position to reveal. Writing σ i \sigma_{i} for the position revealed at step i i , scoring 𝐱 1 : n \mathbf{x}^{1:n} under π \pi amounts to teacher-forcing the true tokens in the order σ \sigma , and p θ π ( 𝐱 1 : n ) = ∏ i = 1 n p θ ( x σ i ∣ x σ < i ) p^{\pi}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{1:n})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_{\theta}(x^{\sigma_{i}}\mid x^{\sigma_{<i}}) is a properly normalized distribution, since σ i \sigma_{i} depends only on x σ < i x^{\sigma_{<i}} . sections.heading: Block diffusion.
sections.text: Full-sequence MDMs cannot generate sequences of arbitrary length and cannot reuse a KV cache. Block diffusion (BD3LM; Arriola et al., 2025 ) partitions 𝐱 1 : n \mathbf{x}^{1:n} into contiguous blocks of b b tokens, factorizes the sequence autoregressively over blocks, and models each block with a masked diffusion model conditioned on the clean prefix. Nearly all large-scale diffusion language models utilize block decomposition now. BD3LM keeps the decoder-only architecture: to score all blocks in one forward pass it concatenates the noised and clean sequences, so a training step runs over 2 ​ n 2n tokens and costs roughly twice the FLOPs of an ARM or MDM step at the same size.

sections.heading: Encoder–decoder block diffusion.
sections.text: E2D2 ( Arriola et al., 2026 ) avoids this overhead by splitting the L L -layer transformer into an L enc L_{\rm enc} -layer encoder that represents the clean prefix and an L dec = L − L enc L_{\rm dec}=L-L_{\rm enc} -layer decoder that denoises the noisy block, attending to its own block by self-attention and to the encoder outputs of the prefix by cross-attention. Each training step is therefore cheaper than a BD3LM step because clean and noised tokens do not go through the same big network.

sections.heading: IsoFLOP scaling laws and the compute multiple.
sections.text: Prior scaling studies of diffusion language models ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Von Rütte et al., 2026 ; Sahoo et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) adopt one IsoFLOP protocol from Hoffmann et al. (2022) : for a fixed training budget C C , a ladder of model sizes N N is trained on D = C / c ⁡ ( N ) D=C/c(N) tokens each, where c ⁡ ( N ) c(N) is the training cost per token. Then, a parabola fitted to the loss against log ⁡ N \log N gives the compute-optimal loss ℒ ∗ ​ ( C ) \mathcal{L}^{\ast}(C) at that budget. Across budgets they fit the power law ℒ ∗ ​ ( C ) = a ​ C α \mathcal{L}^{\ast}(C)=a\,C^{\alpha} by least squares in log–log space. The compute gap between two model families is measured at fixed loss: if family X X reaches loss ℒ \mathcal{L} at budget C X ​ ( ℒ ) C_{X}(\mathcal{L}) and family Y Y at C Y ​ ( ℒ ) C_{Y}(\mathcal{L}) , the compute multiple is C X ​ ( ℒ ) / C Y ​ ( ℒ ) C_{X}(\mathcal{L})/C_{Y}(\mathcal{L}) . It is in this sense that Nie et al. (2025) report a multiple of 16 16 between MDM and ARM.

sections.heading: 3 Scaling law protocol
sections.text: In this section, we introduce our revised scaling law protocol for masked diffusion language models. It inherits the protocol of SMDM ( Nie et al., 2025 ) with two kinds of changes. First, we replace three of SMDM’s choices with more recent alternatives: exact likelihood evaluation, block diffusion at commonly used block sizes, and an encoder–decoder architecture. Second, we correct two aspects of the original SMDM protocol, namely the FLOP count that sets the length of each run and the readout of the compute multiple from the fitted laws. Section 3.1 describes the first kind of changes, and Sections 3.2 and 3.3 state the resulting training and fitting procedure with both corrections included.

sections.heading: Exact likelihood evaluation.
sections.text: We score every diffusion model with DUEL under the top-1 confidence unmasking rule, yielding the exact likelihood induced by this decoding order. To keep the comparison with SMDM, we also score every diffusion model with the ELBO (Eq. 1 , estimated with 128 128 -particle Monte-Carlo), and the ARM with its exact NLL. All models are scored on one frozen validation set of 49,152 49{,}152 sequences, and unless stated otherwise the diffusion models are reported with DUEL.

sections.heading: Block diffusion.
sections.text: In our scaling law analysis protocol, we train block diffusion models at block sizes b ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{4,8,16,32\} . These configurations are chosen from the perspective of language model serving. By the roofline model ( Williams et al., 2009 ) , a GPU becomes compute-bound only above the ratio of its peak throughput to its memory bandwidth; taking BF16 serving as an example, this ratio is about 300 300 FLOPs per byte for an H100 GPU ( NVIDIA, 2023 ) . A block diffusion model decodes up to b b tokens per sequence in one forward pass, which raises the arithmetic intensity to about B ​ b Bb , where B B is the batch size. For mid-size serving with B B between 8 8 and 32 32 , block sizes from 32 32 down to 8 8 thus bring B ​ b Bb to about 256 256 and put the compute units left idle by autoregressive decoding to use, while a larger block adds little throughput. We therefore take b ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{8,16,32\} as the main block sizes, and use b = 4 b{=}4 as a reference for how much training compute a still smaller block can save. These block sizes also match those used to train large diffusion language models: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion ( Fu et al., 2026 ) is trained with b = 32 b{=}32 , Nemotron-TwoTower ( Reda et al., 2026 ) with b = 16 b{=}16 , and SDAR ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) and FLARE ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) with b = 4 b{=}4 (see Table 4 in Appendix A.1 for more models).

sections.heading: Encoder–decoder architecture.
sections.text: Besides decoder-only block diffusion models (BD3LM), we also train encoder–decoder block diffusion models (E2D2) at the same four block sizes in our scaling law analysis protocol. Overall, this gives us ten model variants: ARM, MDM, BD3LM with b ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{4,8,16,32\} and E2D2 with b ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{4,8,16,32\} .

sections.heading: Optimal decoder depth of E2D2.
sections.text: E2D2 has one degree of freedom that the other variants do not have: how the L L layers of a given ladder size are split between the encoder and the decoder, i.e., the decoder fraction L dec / L L_{\rm dec}/L . A wrong split would penalize E2D2 for a reason unrelated to the architecture design itself, so at every grid point of E2D2, i.e., every combination of block size b b , training budget C C and model size N N , we hold the total depth L L fixed and sweep L dec L_{\rm dec} over a wide range. We then report the best DUEL value from the sweep. As a side product, we also analyze how the optimal decoder depth L dec ∗ L^{\ast}_{\rm dec} is related to b b , C C and N N . We believe our results (Section 4.2 ) can give practical guidance on the pretraining of encoder–decoder block diffusion models.

sections.heading: Training recipe.
sections.text: To keep our results consistent with the 16 × 16\times scaling analysis of SMDM, we largely inherit its choices of network architecture, data, tokenizer and hyperparameters. Concretely, all models are LLaMA-style transformers ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) trained on SlimPajama ( Soboleva et al., 2023 ) with a sequence length of 2048 2048 and a batch of 256 × 2048 256\times 2048 tokens. Following SMDM, we use standard parameterization (SP, as opposed to μ \mu P; Yang et al., 2022 ) and AdamW ( β = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) \beta=(0.9,0.95) , weight decay 0.1 0.1 , gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 ) with a peak learning rate of 4 × 10 − 4 4{\times}10^{-4} , a linear warm-up over 1 % 1\% of the steps (at least 100 100 ) and cosine decay to 1 / 10 1/10 of the peak. All diffusion variants use the linear noise schedule α t = 1 − t \alpha_{t}=1-t and, following Sahoo et al. (2026) , the low-variance training loss; following Arriola et al. (2026) , BD3LM and E2D2 draw an independent noise level for every block and always mask at least one token in each block.

sections.heading: IsoFLOP grid.
sections.text: We reuse the size ladder of SMDM (19M–2.1B non-embedding parameters) for all variants and, for each variant, train 7 7 – 10 10 sizes around the compute-optimal size on each of five budgets { 6 × 10 18 , 10 19 , 3 × 10 19 , 6 × 10 19 , 10 20 } \{6{\times}10^{18},10^{19},3{\times}10^{19},6{\times}10^{19},10^{20}\} FLOPs. Across the ten variants, five budgets, sizes per budget and the decoder-depth sweep of E2D2, the grids comprise about 1,700 1{,}700 trained models (approximately 136 136 k B200 GPU hours), more than any prior compute-matched study of diffusion language model scaling that we are aware of.

sections.heading: Compute accounting.
sections.text: At a FLOP budget C C , the length of each run is set by the variant’s training FLOPs per token. SMDM takes this to be 6 ​ N 6N ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) , which is too coarse for a comparison across variants. The 6 ​ N 6N rule ignores the attention score computation entirely, although at our sequence length of 2048 2048 it accounts for a non-negligible fraction of the training FLOPs. More importantly, this fraction differs across variants. We therefore follow Hoffmann et al. (2022) and count the actual training FLOPs, including the output head and the score computation of every attention sublayer (Appendix B.1 gives the per-variant formulas).

sections.heading: Fitting.
sections.text: For each variant we have five budgets C C , each contributing 7 7 – 10 10 sizes N N with their measured NLL (DUEL for the diffusion variants). For each ( variant , C ) (\text{variant},C) we fit a centered parabola in log 10 ⁡ N \log_{10}N to these values and take its vertex, which gives the compute-optimal NLL ℒ ∗ ​ ( C ) \mathcal{L}^{\ast}(C) ; for E2D2, each size contributes only its best L dec L_{\rm dec} . Across budgets we fit the power law ℒ ∗ ​ ( C ) = a ​ C α \mathcal{L}^{\ast}(C)=a\,C^{\alpha} in log–log space, keeping the pure power-law form of prior work so that our numbers are comparable (see further discussion on the law’s functional form in Appendix C.4 ).

sections.heading: Reading the compute multiple.
sections.text: For each diffusion variant we take its compute-optimal NLL ℒ ∗ \mathcal{L}^{\ast} at 10 20 10^{20} FLOPs, find the compute at which the ARM’s fitted law reaches that same ℒ ∗ \mathcal{L}^{\ast} , and take the ratio. Unlike SMDM, we do not extrapolate to do so: given the compute gap between the ARM and the diffusion variants, extrapolating a diffusion law to reach the ARM’s loss lands several times beyond the largest budget we ran, where a small level of noise in the fitted exponent would swing the multiple substantially. Reading the multiple inside the ARM’s measured range instead introduces little noise (see Appendix C.2 for a comparison between the two readouts).

sections.heading: An ELBO baseline in line with 16 × 16\times .
sections.text: With the ELBO readout, our MDM needs 17.8 × 17.8\times the ARM’s compute at 10 20 10^{20} FLOPs, comparable to the 16 × 16\times of Nie et al. (2025) . Although our protocol differs from theirs (in the low-variance training loss, real FLOPs in place of 6 ​ N ​ D 6ND , and the readout), our compute multiple still agrees roughly with their 16 × 16\times . On the same corpus and tokenizer, Sahoo et al. (2026) and Yang et al. (2026) report a smaller ≈ 14 × \approx 14\times for the low-variance MDM, but with a DiT backbone ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) in place of the Llama-style transformer of SMDM that we adopt. This baseline anchors the decomposition that follows.

sections.heading: Exact likelihood readout: the evaluation penalty.
sections.text: Scoring the very same MDM checkpoints with DUEL instead of the ELBO lowers the multiple to 12.8 × 12.8\times . Nothing about the model or its training has changed; about a third of the reported gap is thus an artifact of the evaluation. A reduction is expected: the negative ELBO is an upper bound on the marginal NLL of the MDM whose tightness is poorly understood, whereas DUEL is the exact NLL of the distribution induced by the model’s top-1 confidence decoding rule, and is therefore directly comparable with the ARM’s NLL. This is further supported by extra empirical evidence: in Table 2 , where every diffusion variant is scored both ways, DUEL gives a smaller multiple than the negative ELBO in every case. Beyond likelihood, we also find that DUEL scores higher than the ELBO on multiple-choice benchmarks (Section 4.4 ), further evidence in favor of DUEL than the ELBO.

sections.heading: Block factorization: the first modeling change.
sections.text: The remaining 12.8 × 12.8\times is a genuine training-compute gap, and the next two replacements reduce it by changing how the model is built. Moving from the full-sequence MDM to BD3LM lowers the multiple to 9.6 × 9.6\times at b = 32 b{=}32 , 7.8 × 7.8\times at b = 16 b{=}16 and 5.9 × 5.9\times at b = 8 b{=}8 . Although block-wise training has become common practice ( Bie et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026a ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Reda et al., 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) , this is, to our knowledge, the first controlled, compute-matched demonstration of the benefit of this method in pretraining diffusion language models. We take this as evidence that introducing some degree of left-to-right bias helps language model learning, and that the likelihood gain from the left-to-right block factorization outweighs the penalty of BD3LM’s more expensive training steps, which at matched compute roughly halve the number of steps relative to the MDM. sections.heading: Encoder–decoder architecture: the second modeling change.
sections.text: Moving from BD3LM to E2D2 at the same block size lowers the multiple once more, from 9.6 × 9.6\times to 7.8 × 7.8\times at b = 32 b{=}32 , from 7.8 × 7.8\times to 6.3 × 6.3\times at b = 16 b{=}16 and from 5.9 × 5.9\times to 4.6 × 4.6\times at b = 8 b{=}8 ; at b = 4 b{=}4 it reaches 3.0 × 3.0\times . Note that the decoder-only architecture, inherited from ARMs, remains the convention for diffusion language models: nearly all large-scale DLMs to date, including those trained with block diffusion, use a single decoder-only network ( Nie et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026a ; Fu et al., 2026 ) . Our experiments provide strong evidence that this convention is not the most training-efficient choice for masked diffusion: at matched compute, the encoder–decoder architecture is consistently better, which suggests that it is better suited to the masked diffusion training task. This shows that, for diffusion language models, a conceptual split between encoding and decoding is beneficial: although the encoder and the decoder each have less capacity than the original unified model, letting each concentrate on a different job allows them to use the pretraining compute more efficiently.

sections.heading: 4.2 Where the layers go: optimal decoder depth in E2D2
sections.text: The decoder-depth sweeps of Section 3.1 give the optimal decoder fraction L dec ∗ / L L^{\ast}_{\rm dec}/L at every one of the 142 142 ( b , C , N ) (b,C,N) grid points of E2D2. They lead to a simple conclusion: the optimal decoder fraction depends on the block size alone, and it is decoder-heavy. sections.heading: 4.3 The gap between variants persists beyond the fitting range
sections.text: The laws of Section 4.1 are fitted on five budgets spanning 1.2 1.2 decades, and the natural question is whether the training efficiency gain they describe holds beyond that range. Given the cost of a full sweep at a larger budget, we proceeded as follows: at 3 × 10 20 3{\times}10^{20} FLOPs we trained the ARM and E2D2 at b ∈ { 16 , 32 } b\in\{16,32\} . Each variant was trained at the three ladder sizes that bracket the optimal model size predicted by its law, and E2D2 additionally at three values of L dec L_{\rm dec} centered on the prediction of Eq. 2 . We compare the measured NLL of each variant at the held-out budget with the prediction of the law fitted on the five smaller budgets (Figure 6 ). The gap between variants is reproduced; the absolute laws are not exact. All three variants exhibit a common upward deviation of about 1.1 % 1.1\% ( 24 24 – 28 28 m - nats) from the pure power-law extrapolation, suggesting a mild misspecification of the functional form, which Appendix C.4 traces to a small irreducible term that the five budgets cannot pin down (we therefore conservatively keep the pure power-law form of SMDM and leave fits with an irreducible term to future work). Importantly, the deviation is shared across variants, and the ARM–E2D2 gap is reproduced almost exactly: 261.6 261.6 m - nats measured against 257 257 predicted at b = 16 b{=}16 , and 296.8 296.8 against 294 294 at b = 32 b{=}32 . The quantity this paper is about, the gap between variants, is thus insensitive to the misspecification.

sections.heading: 5 Related work
sections.text: As diffusion language models have attracted attention for their fast, parallel inference, a number of studies have examined how they scale. Nie et al. (2025) were the first to study the scaling of diffusion language models: with IsoFLOP sweeps of MDMs and ARMs on SlimPajama with Llama-style transformers, they found that MDM needs 16 × 16\times the compute of the ARM to reach the same likelihood. Since then, a number of scaling studies of diffusion language models have followed. Sahoo et al. (2026) and Yang et al. (2026) extend the IsoFLOP methodology to other types of diffusion language model: Sahoo et al. (2026) find that uniform-state diffusion needs 23 × 23\times the compute of the ARM, and Yang et al. (2026) find that continuous diffusion needs 20 × 20\times . Von Rütte et al. (2026) measure scaling laws for masked, uniform and hybrid-noise diffusion language models on Nemotron-CC with a CompleteP-parameterized transformer. Interestingly, although they criticize the pure power-law form of Nie et al. (2025) for implicitly assuming a zero irreducible loss, their own fits return an approximately zero irreducible term within their compute range, and they adopt a pure power law in the end. Ni et al. (2025b) refit a Chinchilla-form scaling law for the MDM. Beyond the compute-optimal setting, Prabhudesai et al. (2026) and Ni et al. (2025a) study the scaling of masked diffusion language models in the data-constrained regime and find that, under multi-epoch training, the MDM eventually overtakes the ARM. Our study differs from all of these. To our knowledge, ours is the first to substantially lower the 16 × 16\times figure, revealing that pretraining a diffusion language model from scratch is far cheaper than previously assumed.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper we revisited the scaling laws of diffusion language models, whose widely cited 16 × 16\times compute gap to ARMs ( Nie et al., 2025 ) was measured with a methodology that has fallen out of step with current practice. We revisited and substantially revised their scaling law protocol, proposing to score the model with its exact likelihood, utilize block-aware training and the encoder–decoder architecture, and sweep the commonly used block sizes. In total, we trained about 1,700 1{,}700 models across ten model variants, to our knowledge the largest diffusion language model scaling analysis to date, and found that pretraining diffusion language models is far cheaper than previously thought. Exact likelihood evaluation reduces the compute multiple to 12.8 × 12.8\times ; block diffusion training and an encoder–decoder architecture reduce it further to 7.8 × 7.8\times at block size 32 32 ; and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6 × 4.6\times at block size 8 8 and 3.0 × 3.0\times at block size 4 4 . We complemented these scaling analyses with a simple empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder–decoder block diffusion models, a held-out budget at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmarks where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. In conclusion, the 16 × 16\times figure substantially overstates the compute gap between diffusion and autoregressive language models, and pretraining diffusion language models from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: We hereby list the limitations of this work. Owing to the cost of the grid, all experiments use a single fixed random seed. The held-out budget was not run for b = 8 b{=}8 . When measuring DUEL we use only the top-1 confidence sampler, the default sampler of diffusion language models. The exact likelihood under other unmasking rules may differ. All experiments share one learning-rate and batch-size configuration; although Porian et al. (2024) show that not tuning the hyperparameters at every scale can distort a scaling law, we keep the recipe of Nie et al. (2025) for consistency with the protocol under which the 16 × 16\times was measured. Likewise, we fit pure power laws without an irreducible term for consistency with Nie et al. (2025) ; the consistent miss at the held-out budget suggests that a small irreducible term is present (Appendix C.4 ), and we treat the fitted exponents as local to our compute range. It should be noted that, rather than the exact form of the scaling laws themselves, this paper is more concerned with the comparison between variants.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: In Section 3 , we state the training recipe, the FLOP accounting, the IsoFLOP grids and the readout and fitting procedure in full. sections.heading: A.2 Attention patterns of the model variants
sections.text: Figure 7 illustrates the attention masks of the four model variants on a short sequence, which is what the (query, key) pair counts of Appendix B.1 are derived from. • ARM uses a causal mask: each position attends to itself and to all earlier positions, giving n ⁡ ( n + 1 ) 2 \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2} pairs per layer. • MDM runs full bidirectional attention over the partially masked sequence: every position, masked or not, attends to every other position, giving n 2 n^{2} pairs. • BD3LM keeps the decoder-only architecture but runs a single tower over the length- 2 ​ n 2n concatenation of the clean sequence 𝐱 \mathbf{x} and the noised sequence 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} : the clean half attends block-causally to itself, and each noised block attends to itself and to the clean tokens of all earlier blocks, so that a token can be denoised given its own block and an exact clean prefix; logits are scored on the noised half only. • E2D2 separates the two roles into an encoder and a decoder: the encoder runs block-causal self-attention over the clean sequence, and the decoder runs block-diagonal self-attention within each noised block together with cross-attention to the encoder outputs of the strictly preceding blocks. sections.heading: B.1 FLOP accounting
sections.text: We count real training FLOPs identically for every variant. Unlike 6 ​ N ​ D 6ND , our count includes the output head and the attention score computation. Let n n be the sequence length, d d the width, L L the number of layers, V V the vocabulary size, P P the non-embedding parameter count, and b b the block size; the number of (query, key) pairs per layer depends on the attention mask: causal n ⁡ ( n + 1 ) 2 \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2} , full n 2 n^{2} , block-causal n 2 2 + n ​ b 2 \tfrac{n^{2}}{2}+\tfrac{nb}{2} , block-diagonal n ​ b nb , and block strict-prefix n 2 2 − n ​ b 2 \tfrac{n^{2}}{2}-\tfrac{nb}{2} . For E2D2, the L L layers split into L enc L_{\rm enc} encoder and L dec L_{\rm dec} decoder layers with non-embedding parameter counts P enc P_{\rm enc} and P dec P_{\rm dec} , the latter including the cross-attention projections. For each variant, the per-sample training FLOPs are computed as follows: ARM = 6 ​ P ​ n + 6 ​ d ​ L ​ n ​ ( n + 1 ) + 6 ​ d ​ V ​ n , \displaystyle=6Pn+6dL\,n(n+1)+6dVn, MDM = 6 ​ P ​ n + 12 ​ d ​ L ​ n 2 + 6 ​ d ​ V ​ n , \displaystyle=6Pn+12dL\,n^{2}+6dVn, BD3LM = 12 ​ P ​ n + 12 ​ d ​ L ​ ( n 2 + n ​ b ) + 6 ​ d ​ V ​ n , \displaystyle=12Pn+12dL\,(n^{2}+nb)+6dVn, E2D2 = 6 ​ P enc ​ n + 6 ​ d ​ L enc ​ ( n 2 + n ​ b ) + 6 ​ P dec ​ n + 12 ​ d ​ L dec ​ n ​ b + 6 ​ d ​ L dec ​ ( n 2 − n ​ b ) + 6 ​ d ​ V ​ n . \displaystyle=6P_{\rm enc}n+6dL_{\rm enc}\,(n^{2}+nb)+6P_{\rm dec}n+12dL_{\rm dec}\,nb+6dL_{\rm dec}\,(n^{2}-nb)+6dVn. Table 5 reports the attention score term as a fraction of the per-token training FLOPs for every variant across the size ladder. For BD3LM and E2D2 we take b = 32 b{=}32 as the example, and for E2D2 we additionally set the decoder depth to half the total depth. Two patterns motivate counting real FLOPs rather than using 6 ​ N ​ D 6ND . First, the fraction is sizeable and grows toward smaller models, reaching about 30 % 30\% for the MDM, so 6 ​ N ​ D 6ND distorts the shape of ℒ ∗ ​ ( C ) \mathcal{L}^{\ast}(C) along the ladder. Second, at matched size it differs markedly across variants: the MDM’s full bidirectional attention ( n 2 n^{2} ) costs about twice the ARM’s causal attention ( n 2 / 2 n^{2}/2 ), while E2D2’s decoder attention is the cheapest. An attention-agnostic count therefore mis-charges the variants relative to one another, and this variant-specific difference, unlike terms common to all variants, does not cancel in the compute multiple. sections.heading: Fits with an irreducible term.
sections.text: A pure power law has no irreducible term, whereas the loss is bounded below by the entropy of the data ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , a known weakness of the pure power law ( Von Rütte et al., 2026 ; Ni et al., 2025b ) : a curve that bends towards a floor is under-predicted by a straight line in log–log space, by more the further one extrapolates, which is the signature observed. We therefore refit ℒ ∗ ​ ( C ) = E + a ​ C α \mathcal{L}^{\ast}(C)=E+a\,C^{\alpha} jointly over the eight DUEL variants (ARM, MDM, BD3LM and E2D2 at b ∈ { 4 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{4,16,32\} ) with a single shared E E and per-variant ( a , α ) (a,\alpha) , on the five budgets ≤ 10 20 \leq 10^{20} , and profile the fit over fixed values of E E (Table 14 ). Two observations follow. First, the in-sample rms decreases from 5.9 5.9 m - nats at E = 0 E=0 to 3.1 3.1 at E ≈ 1.5 E\approx 1.5 , so the five budgets favor E > 0 E>0 ; but the minimum is shallow ( 3.1 3.1 – 3.9 3.9 m - nats for E ∈ [ 1.2 , 1.8 ] E\in[1.2,1.8] ), and the exponents move along a ridge with E E , so the five budgets cannot determine the value of E E . Second, adding E ≈ 1.5 E\approx 1.5 removes the miss at the held-out budget: at E = 1.5 E=1.5 the three 3 × 10 20 3{\times}10^{20} cells are predicted to − 7 -7 , + 0.4 +0.4 and 0.0 0.0 m - nats (Figure 10 ). However, the held-out cells come from three sizes bracketing the predicted optimal model size rather than from a full IsoFLOP search, so we do not use them to fix E E , and we conservatively keep the pure power law in the body of the paper, treating its exponents as local to the fitted range. We leave a scaling law with an irreducible term, which would require more budgets to pin down E E , to future work. sections.heading: Benchmark screening.
sections.text: We score the compute-optimal cell of every variant at every budget on all eleven benchmarks. Figure 11 shows, for each benchmark, how the accuracy averaged over the ten variants moves with compute. Eight benchmarks rise with compute by well more than their standard error. WinoGrande and BoolQ do not: on WinoGrande accuracy stays at chance at every budget ( 50.8 % 50.8\% at 10 20 10^{20} FLOPs against a chance level of 50 % 50\% ), and on BoolQ it decreases with compute, so neither can distinguish a better model from a worse one at these scales. COPA does rise with compute, but it has only 100 100 questions, so the standard error of a single COPA accuracy is 4.8 4.8 points, against at most 2 2 points for every other benchmark; in a mean over nine benchmarks, COPA would account for about two-thirds of the variance. We therefore exclude these three benchmarks and use the remaining eight.

We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model’s own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder–decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 1{,}700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8 × 12.8\times ; block diffusion training and an encoder–decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8 × 7.8\times at block size 32 32 , and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6 × 4.6\times at block size 8 8 and 3.0 × 3.0\times at block size 4 4 . Their appeal is fast, parallel generation: open-weight masked diffusion language models report about 2.5 × 2.5\times the generation throughput of autoregressive language models (ARMs) at comparable accuracy ( Wu et al., 2026a ; Reda et al., 2026 ) , with commercial systems reporting up to 10 × 10\times ( Labs et al., 2025 ) . Yet, their training efficiency is widely believed to be far worse than that of ARMs. The most cited quantification is the IsoFLOP study of Nie et al. (2025) (SMDM), which concludes that an MDM needs about 16 × 16\times the training FLOPs of an ARM to reach the same validation perplexity, and the number is now routinely quoted as a property of the MDM family. This 16 × 16\times figure has made pretraining MDMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. Taking a closer look at how this 16 × 16\times figure was achieved, however, we find that the methodology behind it has fallen out of step with current practice of diffusion language modeling. SMDM measured it on a full-sequence, decoder-only MDM scored with its negative evidence lower bound (ELBO), all three of which now have alternatives. First, the ELBO is an upper bound on the negative log-likelihood (NLL), and it scores the model under uniformly random token orders it never uses at inference; in contrast, DUEL ( Turok et al., 2026 ) computes the exact NLL of a diffusion model under the custom decoding order it is deployed with. Second, nearly all of today’s large-scale diffusion language models (DLMs) use block-wise factorization ( Arriola et al., 2025 , BD3LM;) with block sizes between 4 4 and 32 32 , rather than operating over the full sequence. Third, encoder–decoder architectures that separate the processing of clean and noised tokens ( Arriola et al., 2026 , E2D2;) offer computationally cheaper training than the decoder-only network. While the papers that introduce these techniques compare a handful of models at fixed sizes, none of these has been measured under a rigorous compute-matched IsoFLOP analysis. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of masked diffusion models with a protocol that implements the ideas above: we score every diffusion model using the exact likelihood induced by its top-1 confidence decoding rule, utilize block-aware training and an encoder–decoder architecture, and sweep the block sizes b ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{4,8,16,32\} which are commonly used in practice. In addition, we make two corrections to the SMDM protocol: we count training FLOPs exactly, including the output head and attention computation, and we read compute multiples within the measured range of the scaling laws rather than by extrapolation. Under this new protocol we study ten model variants and train about 1,700 1{,}700 models in total; to our knowledge, this is the largest compute-matched scaling analysis of diffusion language models to date. With this analysis, we find that pretraining diffusion language models is far cheaper than previously thought (Figure 1 ). Scored with the ELBO, our full-sequence MDM lands close to the published figure, at 17.8 × 17.8\times . Scoring the very same checkpoints with the exact likelihood lowers the multiple to 12.8 × 12.8\times . Block diffusion training and the encoder–decoder architecture then reduce it further to 7.8 × 7.8\times at block size 32 32 , and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6 × 4.6\times at block size 8 8 and 3.0 × 3.0\times at block size 4 4 . In addition, we find that the optimal decoder depth of encoder–decoder block diffusion follows a simple rule that depends on the block size alone, that the gap between E2D2 and the ARM holds at a held-out budget three times larger than our largest fitted FLOPs, and that likelihood improvements carry over to downstream accuracy. Our contributions are the following. (i) We revisit the scaling laws of diffusion language models under a revised protocol that reflects recent advances: exact likelihood evaluation, block diffusion, encoder–decoder models, and a sweep over practically used block sizes. (ii) We show that, under this protocol, pretraining diffusion language models is far cheaper than the 16 × 16\times suggests: exact likelihood evaluation reduces the compute multiple to 12.8 × 12.8\times , block diffusion training with an encoder–decoder architecture reduces it to 7.8 × 7.8\times at b = 32 b{=}32 , and smaller block sizes further narrow it to 4.6 × 4.6\times at b = 8 b{=}8 and 3.0 × 3.0\times at b = 4 b{=}4 . (iii) We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder–decoder block diffusion, which depends on the block size alone; a held-out budget at 3 × 10 20 3{\times}10^{20} FLOPs, at which the gap between E2D2 and the ARM persists; and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to downstream accuracy. 2 Background Masked diffusion models. It inherits the protocol of SMDM ( Nie et al., 2025 ) with two kinds of changes. First, we replace three of SMDM’s choices with more recent alternatives: exact likelihood evaluation, block diffusion at commonly used block sizes, and an encoder–decoder architecture. Second, we correct two aspects of the original SMDM protocol, namely the FLOP count that sets the length of each run and the readout of the compute multiple from the fitted laws. Section 3.1 describes the first kind of changes, and Sections 3.2 and 3.3 state the resulting training and fitting procedure with both corrections included. 3.1 Incorporating recent advances Exact likelihood evaluation. We score every diffusion model with DUEL under the top-1 confidence unmasking rule, yielding the exact likelihood induced by this decoding order. To keep the comparison with SMDM, we also score every diffusion model with the ELBO (Eq. 1 , estimated with 128 128 -particle Monte-Carlo), and the ARM with its exact NLL. All models are scored on one frozen validation set of 49,152 49{,}152 sequences, and unless stated otherwise the diffusion models are reported with DUEL. Block diffusion. In our scaling law analysis protocol, we train block diffusion models at block sizes b ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{4,8,16,32\} . These configurations are chosen from the perspective of language model serving. By the roofline model ( Williams et al., 2009 ) , a GPU becomes compute-bound only above the ratio of its peak throughput to its memory bandwidth; taking BF16 serving as an example, this ratio is about 300 300 FLOPs per byte for an H100 GPU ( NVIDIA, 2023 ) . A block diffusion model decodes up to b b tokens per sequence in one forward pass, which raises the arithmetic intensity to about B ​ b Bb , where B B is the batch size. For mid-size serving with B B between 8 8 and 32 32 , block sizes from 32 32 down to 8 8 thus bring B ​ b Bb to about 256 256 and put the compute units left idle by autoregressive decoding to use, while a larger block adds little throughput. We therefore take b ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{8,16,32\} as the main block sizes, and use b = 4 b{=}4 as a reference for how much training compute a still smaller block can save. These block sizes also match those used to train large diffusion language models: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion ( Fu et al., 2026 ) is trained with b = 32 b{=}32 , Nemotron-TwoTower ( Reda et al., 2026 ) with b = 16 b{=}16 , and SDAR ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) and FLARE ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) with b = 4 b{=}4 (see Table 4 in Appendix A.1 for more models). Encoder–decoder architecture. Besides decoder-only block diffusion models (BD3LM), we also train encoder–decoder block diffusion models (E2D2) at the same four block sizes in our scaling law analysis protocol. Overall, this gives us ten model variants: ARM, MDM, BD3LM with b ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{4,8,16,32\} and E2D2 with b ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } b\in\{4,8,16,32\} . Optimal decoder depth of E2D2. Nie et al. (2025) were the first to study the scaling of diffusion language models: with IsoFLOP sweeps of MDMs and ARMs on SlimPajama with Llama-style transformers, they found that MDM needs 16 × 16\times the compute of the ARM to reach the same likelihood. Since then, a number of scaling studies of diffusion language models have followed. Sahoo et al. (2026) and Yang et al. (2026) extend the IsoFLOP methodology to other types of diffusion language model: Sahoo et al. (2026) find that uniform-state diffusion needs 23 × 23\times the compute of the ARM, and Yang et al. (2026) find that continuous diffusion needs 20 × 20\times . Von Rütte et al. (2026) measure scaling laws for masked, uniform and hybrid-noise diffusion language models on Nemotron-CC with a CompleteP-parameterized transformer. Interestingly, although they criticize the pure power-law form of Nie et al. (2025) for implicitly assuming a zero irreducible loss, their own fits return an approximately zero irreducible term within their compute range, and they adopt a pure power law in the end. Ni et al. (2025b) refit a Chinchilla-form scaling law for the MDM. Beyond the compute-optimal setting, Prabhudesai et al. (2026) and Ni et al. (2025a) study the scaling of masked diffusion language models in the data-constrained regime and find that, under multi-epoch training, the MDM eventually overtakes the ARM. Our study differs from all of these. To our knowledge, ours is the first to substantially lower the 16 × 16\times figure, revealing that pretraining a diffusion language model from scratch is far cheaper than previously assumed. 6 Conclusion In this paper we revisited the scaling laws of diffusion language models, whose widely cited 16 × 16\times compute gap to ARMs ( Nie et al., 2025 ) was measured with a methodology that has fallen out of step with current practice. We revisited and substantially revised their scaling law protocol, proposing to score the model with its exact likelihood, utilize block-aware training and the encoder–decoder architecture, and sweep the commonly used block sizes. In total, we trained about 1,700 1{,}700 models across ten model variants, to our knowledge the largest diffusion language model scaling analysis to date, and found that pretraining diffusion language models is far cheaper than previously thought. Exact likelihood evaluation reduces the compute multiple to 12.8 × 12.8\times ; block diffusion training and an encoder–decoder architecture reduce it further to 7.8 × 7.8\times at block size 32 32 ; and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6 × 4.6\times at block size 8 8 and 3.0 × 3.0\times at block size 4 4 . We complemented these scaling analyses with a simple empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder–decoder block diffusion models, a held-out budget at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmarks where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. In conclusion, the 16 × 16\times figure substantially overstates the compute gap between diffusion and autoregressive language models, and pretraining diffusion language models from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed. Limitations. We hereby list the limitations of this work. Owing to the cost of the grid, all experiments use a single fixed random seed. The held-out budget was not run for b = 8 b{=}8 . When measuring DUEL we use only the top-1 confidence sampler, the default sampler of diffusion language models. The exact likelihood under other unmasking rules may differ. All experiments share one learning-rate and batch-size configuration; although Porian et al. (2024) show that not tuning the hyperparameters at every scale can distort a scaling law, we keep the recipe of Nie et al. (2025) for consistency with the protocol under which the 16 × 16\times was measured. Likewise, we fit pure power laws without an irreducible term for consistency with Nie et al. (2025) ; the consistent miss at the held-out budget suggests that a small irreducible term is present (Appendix C.4 ), and we treat the fitted exponents as local to our compute range. It should be noted that, rather than the exact form of the scaling laws themselves, this paper is more concerned with the comparison between variants.
